sections.title: Epidemiology, risk factors and inherited predisposition

blocks.text: Worldwide, breast cancer is **second only to lung cancer in incidence** and is the **leading cause of cancer death in women** (Davidson). US-based review books describe it as the commonest cancer in women and the second cause of female cancer death after lung. Fewer than 1% of cases occur in men. Most tumours arise from the **epithelium of the milk ducts and lobules**.

Oestrogen makes duct epithelium divide through the **cyclin D1–CDK complex, which phosphorylates Rb** and pushes cells from G1 into S phase. Years of oestrogen-driven division give more chances for replication errors, so a long **lifetime oestrogen exposure** raises risk. Disordered control of this same pathway drives ER-positive cancers, and it is the target of CDK4/6 inhibitors.

blocks.title: Risk factors
rows: Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, prolonged HRT
Obesity (postmenopausal), alcohol; smoking is listed by some sources
Increasing age, previous breast cancer, affected first-degree relative
Previous chest irradiation, e.g. mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma
Raised risk with atypia (atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia) or proliferative change; no added risk with simple cysts, simple fibroadenoma or columnar change
Far Eastern migrants start at low risk, but risk rises over later generations toward the host-country rate (diet, later first pregnancy, lifestyle)

blocks.title: Inherited predisposition
rows: Breast, ovary, colon, prostate, pancreas. Lifetime breast risk about 35–85%
Sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast, leukaemia, glioma, adrenocortical
Leukaemia, lymphoma and several solid tumours; the AT gene also predisposes to breast cancer
PALB2 about 35% by age 70; CHEK2/BARD1 moderate risk (15–30% lifetime)

blocks.title: Numbers to know
items: About **5–10% of breast cancers are hereditary** (Davidson); Kumar quotes about 5%, Washington under 10%.
BRCA protein is a **DNA-repair tumour suppressor**. Male BRCA carriers risk male breast cancer, and BRCA2 men also risk prostate cancer.
Washington gives cumulative breast cancer risk by age 70 as about 57% (BRCA1) and 49% (BRCA2).

blocks.text: **Refer for genetic counselling** when the patient is young, is male, or has a strong family history: a mother or sister diagnosed before 40, a father or brother at any age, bilateral disease with the first before 50, breast plus ovarian cancer in close relatives, or an Ashkenazi Jewish relative with breast or ovarian cancer. Germline testing is also advised for metastatic or triple-negative disease and diagnosis at 45 or younger.

The **combined oral contraceptive** is not a proven risk factor: Davidson finds no definite evidence of a link and Pocket Medicine calls the risk very low or absent. But once a woman **has** breast cancer, hormonal contraception is contraindicated, and the copper IUD is the safest choice.

Screening works because cancer can stay **in situ** for a long time. While malignant duct cells have not breached the **basement membrane**, they cannot reach the lymphatics, so screen-detected disease is highly curable. Screening mammography cuts breast cancer mortality by roughly **20–30%**, with a smaller absolute gain under 50.

blocks.title: Screening programmes
rows: Biplanar digital mammography every 3 years, with recall for abnormal films. Women over 65 are not routinely invited but can ask; uptake is low even though incidence rises with age
Mammography every 2 years from 50 to 75 (some start at 40)
Yearly from 45, with the option of every 2 years after 54
Start earlier: age 25 for BRCA carriers, 5–10 years before the youngest affected relative, 8–10 years after thoracic radiotherapy
Add if lifetime risk is over 20% (BRCA carrier, strong family history, previous chest radiotherapy)

blocks.title: Risk reduction in high-risk women
rows: Lowers invasive cancer risk; raises DVT and uterine cancer risk; contraindicated in pregnancy
Postmenopausal only; less effective than tamoxifen; also lowers vertebral fracture risk; raises DVT/PE and stroke risk
Postmenopausal only; cuts risk by more than half; causes osteoporosis
BRCA carriers; lowers both ovarian and breast cancer risk

blocks.text: Ultrasound, not mammography, is used in young women because their **dense breast tissue** hides lesions on a mammogram. MRI is more sensitive than mammography in high-risk and young women.

For prevention, **tamoxifen** works in pre- and postmenopausal women, but **raloxifene and aromatase inhibitors are postmenopausal only**. Both SERMs raise venous thromboembolism risk, so a woman with a previous PE is better suited to an aromatase inhibitor.

sections.title: Pathology: in situ, invasive and molecular types

blocks.text: **Carcinoma in situ** is confined within the duct or lobule and has not invaded the stroma. **Invasive carcinoma** has crossed the basement membrane and can spread through lymphatics and blood.

blocks.title: DCIS vs LCIS
rows: Screening mammogram (often microcalcification), with or without a mass; about 20% of screen-detected cancers
Incidental finding on a biopsy taken for another lesion; rarely palpable
Precursor: invasion in 10% at 5 years after excision alone, usually in the same breast
Risk marker: cancer in either breast in about 7% at 10 years
Pure DCIS does not spread to nodes
Lumpectomy (mastectomy if clear margins impossible) ± radiotherapy; tamoxifen if ER-positive
Observation, SERM chemoprevention or prophylactic bilateral mastectomy; excising it does not lower the risk

blocks.title: Invasive histological types
rows: About 70% (70–80% in Pocket Medicine): the commonest
Metaplastic, adenoid cystic, secretory, apocrine; Paget's disease of the nipple; phyllodes tumour (a sarcoma)

blocks.text: **Molecular subtypes** (Davidson): **luminal A, luminal B, HER2-type and basal-like**. Basal-like tumours are usually **triple negative** (ER−, PR−, HER2−). In Washington, about **75% are ER-positive** (good prognosis, endocrine-responsive), PR usually follows ER, about **20% are HER2-positive** (higher grade) and **10–15% are triple negative** (aggressive, with no endocrine or HER2 target).
Histological **type** has little prognostic value on its own. Tumour **grade** matters more, along with nodal status and receptor status.

**Inflammatory carcinoma is not a histological type.** It is a clinical picture produced by tumour in the **dermal lymphatics**, and the prognosis is very poor. **Paget's disease of the nipple** is ductal carcinoma spreading into the nipple epidermis and is linked to underlying DCIS.
If a **node is positive in a case of "pure" DCIS** (about 2% of cases where nodes are sampled), there is an **undetected invasive focus**. DCIS itself does not metastasise.

**The sources disagree on HER2 frequency.** Davidson says HER2 is overexpressed in about **one-third** of breast cancers, while Kumar and Washington give about **20%**. Quote Davidson in a Davidson-based exam, and know that HER2-positive disease is aggressive but treatable with targeted drugs.

sections.title: Clinical features and patterns of spread

blocks.text: Most cancers are found by **screening** or present as a **painless, enlarging lump**. **Nipple discharge** occurs in about 10% and **pain** in about 7%. A malignant lump is typically **hard, irregular, fixed and non-tender**, and about 60% arise in the **upper outer quadrant**. Nipple discharge is suspicious when it is unilateral, from a single duct, bloody or accompanied by a mass.

blocks.title: Examination: what to document
items: Position of the lesion and its **size in centimetres**
Tethering: **superficial** (skin dimpling) or **deep** (to pectoralis)
To test deep tethering, the patient presses her hands inward on her iliac crests to tense pectoralis; a deeply tethered mass becomes **immobile**
Nipple discharge or retraction, skin oedema (**peau d'orange**), redness or ulceration
**Axillary** and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy

blocks.title: Special and advanced presentations
rows: Long-standing **unilateral eczematous, scaly erosion** of the nipple spreading to the areola, with or without discharge; underlying DCIS
Rare and aggressive: red, warm, heavy, painful breast with diffuse skin induration and peau d'orange, usually with axillary nodes; poor prognosis
Axillary nodes, peau d'orange, fixation to skin or chest wall

blocks.title: Spread (Davidson)
rows: About 40% at diagnosis; more likely with larger primaries
70% of metastatic cases: progressive pain, **worse at night**; breast causes **53% of all pathological fractures**
60% / 40%: cough, dyspnoea; lung and breast are the commonest causes of malignant effusion
10–20%: breast causes 15% of brain metastases (lung 48%), and these patients do better than those with other primaries

blocks.title: Metabolic and paraneoplastic links
items: **Hypercalcaemia** from bone metastases or from **PTHrP**, a pattern shared with myeloma and kidney cancer
Breast cancer is a recognised cause of **neurological paraneoplastic syndromes**
A **malignant pleural effusion** means advanced, incurable disease

blocks.text: **Breast cancer is rare under 35.** A round, mobile lump that changes with the menstrual cycle in a young woman suggests **fibroadenoma**. **Fat necrosis** after trauma (often forgotten) mimics cancer clinically and on mammography; biopsy shows foamy macrophages and coarse calcification.

Every symptomatic lump gets **triple assessment**: **clinical examination**, **imaging** (mammography, ultrasound, MRI when needed) and **cytology or histology**. Benign lumps outnumber cancers by about **15 to 1**, so the three parts must agree. **Any clinically suspicious mass is biopsied whatever the imaging shows.**

blocks.alt: Algorithm: breast lump work-up. Clinical examination, then age-based imaging (ultrasound under 30, mammogram at 30 or over), then tissue diagnosis; concordant benign results allow reassurance, while any suspicious element leads to biopsy and staging.

blocks.title: Imaging and tissue sampling
rows: First test under 30 (dense breasts); tells a cyst from a solid mass. Malignant features: hypoechoic, taller than wide, posterior acoustic shadowing
First test at 30 or over or after menopause. Red flags: spiculated or irregular mass, clustered microcalcifications, enlarging lesion
High-risk screening; axillary nodal cancer with no breast lesion on routine imaging (to find an occult primary)
Quick, but a small sample with a **high false-negative rate**; cannot give receptor status reliably
Histology, **grade**, **Ki-67**, **ER/PR/HER2**; stereotactic guidance for an impalpable mammographic lesion
Indeterminate result or atypia on core biopsy

blocks.title: Biomarkers and markers
items: **ER/PR** positivity on immunohistochemistry predicts response to **endocrine therapy**.
High **HER2** expression predicts response to **trastuzumab**. **FISH** detects HER2 gene amplification.
**Oncotype DX** (21-gene recurrence score) in ER+/HER2− disease (node-negative or 1–3 nodes) picks out women who gain little from chemotherapy.
**CA15-3** (with CEA or CA27-29) tracks response in metastatic or recurrent disease. It is **not a diagnostic test**.

blocks.title: Staging work-up
items: Staging uses **TNM**: tumour size and local invasion, regional nodes, distant metastases.
Axilla: **sentinel node** mapping with blue dye or a radioactive tracer.

Distant staging (**CT thorax/abdomen and isotope bone scan**) is done when spread is suspected, routinely for **stage III or above**, and in stage I–II only if there are new symptoms or abnormal blood tests.
**PET–CT** is the most sensitive test in advanced disease (Kumar). First Aid also lists chest imaging, CT, brain MRI and bone scan for metastatic disease.

blocks.title: Stage and 5-year survival
rows: Tumour 2–5 cm and/or mobile axillary nodes (IIA: over 2 cm or mobile nodes; IIB: over 5 cm, or 2–5 cm with mobile nodes)
Fixed axillary or internal mammary nodes (IIIA); chest wall or skin involvement, or infra/supraclavicular nodes (IIIB/C)

blocks.text: **Axillary nodal status is the strongest single prognostic factor**, and overall TNM stage is the most reliable predictor. ER/PR positivity is favourable. Patients with ECOG performance status 3–4 do worse than those at 0–2.

**Ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes are stage III (IIIB/C, locoregional), not stage IV.** First Aid lists them as stage IV, but the AJCC-based table in Pocket Medicine places them in IIIB/C. Node-only disease can still be treated with curative intent.

Nodal figures differ: Davidson says about **40%** have axillary nodal disease at diagnosis, while Kumar says only **20%** are free of **microscopic** nodal deposits. Quote Davidson's 40% for clinically relevant nodal disease.

blocks.note: Look at: spiculated mammographic mass with a satellite lesion (MLO and CC views), and a hypoechoic, taller-than-wide mass with posterior acoustic shadowing on ultrasound.

blocks.text: **Surgery is the mainstay** of treatment for operable disease. Options range from **lumpectomy / wide local excision** to **mastectomy**. **Breast-conserving surgery (BCS) is as effective as mastectomy** if the tumour is completely excised with **negative margins** and the breast is then irradiated. Kumar uses about **3 cm** as a guide for conservation; larger tumours need simple mastectomy, with or without reconstruction. The axilla is staged at the same operation.

blocks.title: When mastectomy is preferred over BCS
rows: Large tumour relative to the breast; multicentric disease; diffuse or extensive microcalcification
Subareolar tumour; involvement of nipple or overlying skin; fixation to chest wall

blocks.title: Managing the axilla
items: Clinically and ultrasound-negative axilla: **sentinel lymph node biopsy**. A negative sentinel node **avoids axillary clearance**.
Clinically involved nodes: **axillary dissection** (to level III) for local control and prognostic information.
The more axillary surgery, the higher the risk of **arm lymphoedema**.

blocks.title: Radiotherapy
rows: **Always**: whole-breast radiotherapy with a boost to the tumour bed, giving local control equal to mastectomy. Adjuvant radiotherapy lowers local recurrence to about **4–6%**
Chest wall ± regional nodes if: 4 or more positive nodes, tumour over 5 cm, positive or close margins, or skin/chest wall involvement
A dissected axilla is **not** irradiated (lymphoedema risk), but the supraclavicular fossa is included
Palliation of painful bone metastases and brain metastases

blocks.text: **Neoadjuvant systemic therapy** (chemotherapy ± HER2-directed therapy, or endocrine therapy) can **shrink a locally advanced tumour** enough to allow breast conservation instead of mastectomy.

**Radiotherapy toxicity**: acute skin reactions are common towards the end of breast or chest wall treatment and settle within weeks. **Late effects** appear 6 weeks or more after treatment in 5–10% of patients and include **brachial plexus damage** and **subcutaneous fibrosis**.

The books set different conditions for BCS. Davidson's only condition is **complete excision with clear margins** (plus radiotherapy); Kumar adds a size guide of about 3 cm. In an exam, **clear margins + radiotherapy = equivalent to mastectomy**.

sections.title: Systemic therapy for early disease: endocrine, chemotherapy and targeted drugs

blocks.text: **Adjuvant** therapy is given after surgery and radiotherapy to destroy **micrometastases**. **Neoadjuvant** therapy is given first, to downstage the tumour and show whether it responds, with the same overall survival. Adjuvant therapy clearly improves survival in **node-positive, large, ER-negative and HER2-positive** cancers.

blocks.title: Who gets what (adjuvant)
rows: Higher risk: tumour over 1 cm, ER-negative, involved nodes
Adjuvant **chemotherapy**, which improves disease-free and overall survival
Oncotype DX guides chemotherapy; low and mid-range scores (0–25) gain no significant benefit
HER2+ (1 cm or more, or node-positive)
**Trastuzumab** (± pertuzumab) **with chemotherapy**, then endocrine therapy if also ER+
Chemotherapy (First Aid: if tumour over 0.5 cm); pembrolizumab may be added

blocks.title: Endocrine therapy
rows: Competitive ER blocker; works before and after menopause; 10 years beats 5
Antagonist in breast but **agonist in endometrium**: hot flushes, **endometrial cancer**, **VTE**
Block peripheral (non-ovarian) conversion of androgens to oestrogen; **postmenopausal** standard adjuvant therapy; slightly better than tamoxifen
Ovarian suppression for premenopausal ER+ disease; combined with tamoxifen or an AI in higher risk or age 35 or under
ER antagonist that also **degrades** the receptor; postmenopausal / metastatic disease

blocks.text: **AIs do not work before the menopause** unless the ovaries are suppressed. Davidson advises an **LHRH analogue** for premenopausal ER+ women, calls adjuvant AIs promising but under investigation, and places AIs second-line in metastatic disease. Kumar, Pocket Medicine and Washington make an AI the **first-line adjuvant drug after the menopause**. Endocrine therapy runs 5–10 years.

blocks.title: Chemotherapy
items: Combinations of drugs with **non-overlapping toxicities** reduce resistance.
Adjuvant therapy is usually an **anthracycline ± a taxane**. Alkylating agents, 5-FU and vinca alkaloids also feature in first-line regimens.
In **triple-negative** disease, **platinum** drugs also have a role.

blocks.title: Targeted therapies
rows: With chemotherapy in HER2+ disease; trastuzumab markedly reduces relapse
T-DM1 for residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy and as second-line in metastatic disease; deruxtecan is more effective but causes more lung toxicity
With an AI or fulvestrant in ER+ disease
Everolimus with exemestane; alpelisib with fulvestrant if PIK3CA-mutant

blocks.text: **Cardiotoxicity**: anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiomyopathy is **dose-related**, so keep the cumulative dose within about **450 mg/m² doxorubicin-equivalent**. **Trastuzumab** can also cause heart failure, **especially combined with doxorubicin**, and radiotherapy adds to the risk. Epirubicin or liposomal doxorubicin lowers the risk. Monitor cardiac function during HER2 therapy.

blocks.note: Look at: anthracycline-induced dilated cardiomyopathy with congestive heart failure, a cardiotoxicity of breast chemotherapy that trastuzumab makes worse.

blocks.text: Metastatic breast cancer is usually **not curable** (5-year survival about 18% for stage IV in Davidson), but treatment can **prolong life with good quality** for long periods. The plan depends on **receptor status, tumour burden and pace**.

blocks.title: Matching treatment to the situation
rows: **Endocrine therapy first**: an AI plus a **CDK4/6 inhibitor** as first line. Chemotherapy is kept for progression, with no loss of overall survival
Widespread or high-burden visceral disease, or HR-negative
**Chemotherapy** (± anti-HER2 therapy), then endocrine therapy if ER+
Chemotherapy ± a checkpoint inhibitor (PD-L1+); **PARP inhibitor** if BRCA-mutant
Oligometastatic disease in a fit patient
Possibly curable with ablative focal therapy: radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic radiotherapy or metastatectomy
Curative intent: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery, regional radiotherapy and long-term endocrine/HER2 therapy
Prefer drugs the tumour has not yet seen (e.g. **eribulin**). Re-biopsy or cfDNA may show new drivers such as **PI3K** pathway mutations

blocks.title: Later endocrine options
items: Davidson positions **aromatase inhibitors** as second-line endocrine therapy in metastatic disease. They act on oestrogen made in adrenal and adipose tissue.
**Progestogens** (e.g. megestrol acetate) are used once disease has progressed on standard anti-oestrogen therapy.
**Fulvestrant**, and **everolimus** with exemestane, are further endocrine-based options.

blocks.title: Complications of metastases
rows: **IV bisphosphonates** (pamidronate, zoledronic acid) or **denosumab** reduce pain, fractures and hypercalcaemia; external-beam radiotherapy or strontium; endocrine therapy or chemotherapy
Impending fracture (large lytic lesion with over 50% cortical loss in a weight-bearing bone)
IV fluids, then bisphosphonate or denosumab
Aspirate; if the effusion is the presenting feature of breast cancer, give systemic chemotherapy; pleurodesis if it recurs
Dexamethasone for oedema, radiotherapy (whole-brain or stereotactic), surgery for a single lesion

blocks.text: **PARP inhibitors** (olaparib) block single-strand break repair. In a **BRCA-mutant** tumour, double-strand repair is already defective, so losing both pathways kills the cell (**synthetic lethality**) while sparing normal tissue.

**Follow-up** after treatment is mainly clinical. Routine scanning is not supported. **Annual mammography of both breasts** is advised for at least 10 years, because the other breast carries a higher risk of a new cancer.
**Bevacizumab** (anti-VEGF-A) slowed progression of metastatic breast cancer, but its breast licence was **revoked** because it did little for survival or quality of life.

cards.front: What fraction of breast cancers is hereditary (Davidson), and which genes are involved?
cards.back: About **5–10%**: BRCA1, BRCA2, AT and TP53

cards.front: Which inherited syndromes predispose to breast cancer?
cards.back: BRCA1/2, Li–Fraumeni (TP53), Cowden syndrome (PTEN), Peutz–Jeghers (STK11), ataxia telangiectasia

cards.front: Which hormonal factors raise breast cancer risk?
cards.back: Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy and prolonged HRT (long oestrogen exposure). The OCP has no definite link

cards.front: UK breast screening method and interval?
cards.back: Biplanar digital mammography **every 3 years**, with recall for abnormal films. Women over 65 can ask for it but are not routinely invited

cards.front: When is annual MRI screening added?
cards.back: Lifetime risk over **20%**: BRCA carriers, strong family history, previous chest radiotherapy. BRCA carriers start at 25

cards.front: Key DCIS numbers (Davidson)?
cards.back: About 20% of screen-detected cancers; multifocal in one-third; invasion in 10% at 5 years after excision alone; pure DCIS does not spread to nodes

cards.front: What does LCIS signify?
cards.back: A **risk marker** for invasive cancer in **either** breast (about 7% at 10 years); usually found incidentally

cards.front: Define triple-negative breast cancer.
cards.back: ER−, PR− and HER2−; usually the basal-like subtype; about 10–15%; aggressive, with no endocrine or HER2 target

cards.front: Commonest sites of distant breast metastasis (Davidson)?
cards.back: Bone is commonest (70%), ahead of lung (60%) and liver (55%); then pleura 40%, adrenal 35%, skin 30% and brain 10–20%

cards.front: Paget's disease of the nipple: features?
cards.back: Unilateral eczematous, scaly nipple erosion spreading to the areola, with or without discharge; underlying DCIS / ductal cancer

cards.front: What are the three parts of triple assessment?
cards.back: Clinical examination + imaging (mammography/ultrasound ± MRI) + cytology or core biopsy

cards.front: First imaging test for a breast lump by age?
cards.back: Under 30: **ultrasound** (dense breasts). 30 or over / postmenopausal: **mammogram**

cards.front: 5-year survival by stage (Davidson)?
Indications for post-mastectomy radiotherapy?
cards.back: 4 or more positive nodes, tumour over 5 cm, positive/close margins, skin or chest wall involvement

cards.front: Clinically node-negative axilla with a negative sentinel node: next step?
cards.back: No axillary clearance (this avoids lymphoedema). Clinically involved nodes need axillary dissection

cards.front: Why are aromatase inhibitors not used alone before the menopause?
cards.back: They block only **non-ovarian** oestrogen synthesis, so they work only with ovarian suppression

cards.front: Main toxicities of tamoxifen?
cards.back: Hot flushes, **endometrial cancer** and **VTE** (agonist in endometrium, antagonist in breast)

cards.front: Safe cumulative anthracycline limit and modifiers?
cards.back: Within about **450 mg/m²** doxorubicin-equivalent; risk rises with trastuzumab or radiotherapy; lower with epirubicin or liposomal doxorubicin

cards.front: Drugs that cut skeletal events from bone metastases?
cards.back: IV bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronic acid) or denosumab

cards.front: First-line treatment for indolent ER+ metastatic disease?
cards.back: An aromatase inhibitor plus a **CDK4/6 inhibitor** (e.g. palbociclib); chemotherapy waits for progression

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has a high-grade breast cancer. Her younger brother had an osteosarcoma of the femur at 14, her mother died of an adrenocortical carcinoma and a cousin was treated for a glioma.
items.explanation: Childhood sarcoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, brain tumour and early breast cancer together point to **Li–Fraumeni syndrome**, caused by germline **TP53** mutation (AD).

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with breast cancer had freckle-like pigmented macules on her lips and buccal mucosa as a child, and needed surgery at 15 for an ileal intussusception caused by hamartomatous polyps.
items.explanation: Mucocutaneous pigmentation and small-bowel hamartomas mean **Peutz–Jeghers syndrome** (STK11). Davidson links it to colonic, ileal, breast and ovarian cancer.

items.stem: A 58-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish man has a hard lump behind his left nipple, and biopsy confirms breast carcinoma. His brother was treated for prostate cancer at 52.
items.explanation: Two steps: **male breast cancer** in an Ashkenazi family should prompt BRCA testing. Of the two BRCA genes, **BRCA2** carries the added prostate cancer risk in men.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman asks about breast screening. At 18 she had mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. She has no family history of breast cancer and her clinical breast examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which screening plan is most appropriate for her?
options: Annual MRI with mammography, starting now
No screening, because she has no family history
questions.explanation: Previous **chest irradiation** puts her lifetime risk above 20%. That justifies **annual MRI** with mammography, starting **8–10 years after thoracic radiotherapy**, which she has already passed.
whyNot: Population screening from 50 is for average-risk women and starts too late for her.
Examination alone is not a screening tool for a high-risk woman.
Ultrasound is the diagnostic test for a lump in a young woman, not a high-risk screening programme.
Her risk comes from radiation, not family history.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman has lobular carcinoma in situ on a biopsy taken for a benign lesion. She wants to lower her risk of invasive cancer. Two years ago she had a pulmonary embolism, and her bone density is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which risk-reducing drug is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Both SERMs (tamoxifen, raloxifene) **raise venous thromboembolism risk**, which matters after her PE. In a **postmenopausal** woman, an **aromatase inhibitor** cuts breast cancer risk by more than half. Its main drawback is osteoporosis, and her bones are normal.
whyNot: Tamoxifen raises DVT/PE risk and uterine cancer risk.
Raloxifene also raises DVT/PE risk and is less effective than tamoxifen.
HRT increases breast cancer risk.
Progestogens are used in metastatic disease after anti-oestrogen failure, not for prevention.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman is recalled after routine screening because of a segment of clustered microcalcifications. There is no palpable mass. Core biopsy shows malignant cells filling the ducts, with an intact basement membrane.
items.explanation: Malignant cells confined within the ducts and found as **microcalcification on screening** mean **DCIS**. It makes up about 20% of screen-detected cancers.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a fibroadenoma excised. The pathologist reports an incidental, non-invasive proliferation filling the acini of nearby lobules. She is told her risk of invasive cancer is raised in **both** breasts and that wider excision would not remove that risk.
items.explanation: An incidental lobular in situ lesion that raises risk in **either** breast (about 7% at 10 years) is **LCIS**. Excising it does not lower the risk.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has a scaly, weeping, eczema-like rash confined to one nipple for 4 months. It has spread to the areola and not improved with a topical steroid. Biopsy shows malignant cells within the epidermis.
items.explanation: A unilateral nipple "eczema" that does not respond to treatment is **Paget's disease of the nipple**: ductal carcinoma cells in the nipple epidermis, usually with underlying DCIS.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old student has a 2 cm smooth, rubbery lump that slips away under the fingers. She thinks it gets slightly bigger before her periods. There are no skin changes or axillary nodes.
items.explanation: A young woman with a **round, very mobile lump that changes with the cycle** has a **fibroadenoma**. Cancer is rare under 35.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman was the front-seat passenger in a car crash 2 months ago. She now has a firm, irregular lump in the upper inner breast with slight skin dimpling, and the mammogram is reported as suspicious. Core biopsy shows foamy macrophages and coarse calcification.
items.explanation: Trauma (here, likely a seat-belt injury) followed by a hard, irregular lump that mimics cancer, with **foamy macrophages** on biopsy, means **fat necrosis**.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman who is not breastfeeding has a red, warm, swollen and heavy left breast. The skin is thickened and pitted like orange peel, and there is a hard axillary node. A week of antibiotics has made no difference and she has no fever.
items.explanation: Diffuse erythema and **peau d'orange** with axillary nodes, unresponsive to antibiotics in a non-lactating woman, is **inflammatory carcinoma**. It reflects tumour in the dermal lymphatics. Confirm with a full-thickness skin biopsy.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has a painless, hard, irregular 3 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant. It dimples the skin when she raises her arm, and it becomes fixed when she presses her hands into her hips.
items.explanation: A **hard, irregular, painless lump** in the upper outer quadrant with skin tethering and **deep fixation to pectoralis** is a breast carcinoma until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a 2 cm discrete, mobile lump in the right breast that has persisted through two menstrual cycles.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first imaging test?
questions.explanation: Under 30, **dense breast tissue** makes mammography unreliable. **Ultrasound** comes first and separates a cyst from a solid lump. Imaging is one part of triple assessment.
whyNot: Mammography is the first test at 30 or over, or after the menopause.
MRI is for high-risk screening or an occult primary, not first-line.
CT is a staging test, not a diagnostic test for a lump.
A bone scan is for staging suspected metastases.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm hard lump. Mammography shows a spiculated mass. Treatment decisions will depend on tumour grade and receptor status.
questions.leadIn: Which test should be done next?
options: Wide local excision of the mass
questions.explanation: When cancer is likely, a **large-bore core biopsy** gives histology, **grade, Ki-67 and ER/PR/HER2 status**. These decide endocrine, chemotherapy and anti-HER2 treatment.
whyNot: FNA gives cytology only, has a high false-negative rate and is a poor source for receptor status.
CA15-3 monitors metastatic disease; it is not a diagnostic test.
PET–CT is for advanced-disease staging, not tissue diagnosis.
Definitive surgery comes after the tissue diagnosis: grade and receptor status decide whether neoadjuvant therapy is needed and how the operation is planned.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.
options: Wide local excision, sentinel node biopsy and whole-breast radiotherapy
Mastectomy with axillary dissection and chest wall radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant systemic therapy followed by surgery

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm invasive ductal carcinoma in a medium-sized breast. The axilla is normal on examination and ultrasound. She wants to keep her breast.
items.explanation: A small unifocal tumour can be treated by **breast conservation**, with clear margins, sentinel node staging and **whole-breast radiotherapy**. This is equivalent to mastectomy.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has a 2 cm invasive cancer, but mammography shows **diffuse suspicious microcalcification across three quadrants**, and biopsies from separate quadrants confirm malignancy. The axilla is clinically and sonographically normal.
items.explanation: Multicentric disease and diffuse microcalcification are contraindications to BCS, so she needs **mastectomy**. The axilla is clinically negative, so it is staged with a **sentinel node biopsy**.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 6 cm HER2-positive tumour with matted, fixed axillary nodes. Staging CT and bone scan show no distant spread.
items.explanation: This is locally advanced (stage III) disease. **Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with HER2-directed therapy** comes first to downstage it, then surgery and radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman has a 1.5 cm ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer treated with wide local excision and radiotherapy. A junior doctor suggests letrozole alone as adjuvant endocrine therapy.
questions.leadIn: Why is letrozole alone inappropriate for her?
options: It blocks only non-ovarian oestrogen synthesis, so ovarian oestrogen is unaffected
It is an antagonist that degrades the oestrogen receptor
It causes endometrial cancer in premenopausal women
It acts only on HER2-positive tumours
It must always be combined with chemotherapy
questions.explanation: Aromatase inhibitors block **peripheral (non-ovarian)** conversion of androgens to oestrogen. Before the menopause the ovaries keep making oestrogen, so an AI only works **with ovarian suppression** (LHRH agonist or oophorectomy). Tamoxifen is the standard alternative.
whyNot: That describes fulvestrant.
Endometrial cancer is a tamoxifen effect (agonist action on the endometrium).
Letrozole is endocrine therapy for ER-positive disease; HER2 status is irrelevant to it.
Endocrine therapy is used without chemotherapy in low-risk ER+ disease.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer had adjuvant doxorubicin-based chemotherapy and is now on trastuzumab. Over 3 weeks she develops exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea and ankle swelling. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: **Anthracycline cardiomyopathy** is dose-related, and **trastuzumab can itself cause heart failure, especially after or with doxorubicin**. Their combination is the classic cause of cardiotoxicity in breast cancer.
whyNot: Taxanes are mainly neurotoxic.
Tamoxifen causes VTE and endometrial cancer, not cardiomyopathy.
AIs cause osteoporosis.
Bisphosphonates do not cause dilated cardiomyopathy.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.
options: Aromatase inhibitor plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor
IV fluids then an IV bisphosphonate
Ablative focal therapy (e.g. stereotactic radiotherapy or resection)

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman treated for ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer 6 years ago has mild aching in her spine. A bone scan shows several metastases. She has no visceral disease and is otherwise well.
items.explanation: Indolent, non-life-threatening **ER+** metastatic disease: **endocrine therapy first**, now an AI plus a **CDK4/6 inhibitor**. Chemotherapy is kept for progression.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with known bone metastases has become confused, thirsty and constipated. Her corrected calcium is 3.4 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Symptomatic **hypercalcaemia** of malignancy: rehydrate with **IV fluids**, then give an **IV bisphosphonate** (or denosumab).

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer had 2 L of malignant pleural fluid aspirated 3 weeks ago. She is breathless again, and the chest X-ray shows the effusion has re-accumulated.
items.explanation: A **recurrent** malignant effusion after initial drainage should be treated with **pleurodesis**.

items.stem: A fit 52-year-old woman, 4 years after curative treatment, has a single 2 cm liver metastasis. Full staging shows no other disease.
items.explanation: This is **oligometastatic** disease in a fit patient. Ablative focal therapy (stereotactic radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or metastatectomy) still offers a chance of cure.

questions.theme: Adverse effects of breast cancer treatment
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has taken tamoxifen for 4 years. She now has postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, and transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium.
items.explanation: Tamoxifen is an **agonist in the endometrium**. Postmenopausal bleeding in a tamoxifen user means **endometrial carcinoma** until proven otherwise.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has taken anastrozole for 3 years. She fractures her wrist falling from standing height, and DEXA shows a T-score of −3.0.
items.explanation: Aromatase inhibitors deplete oestrogen and cause **osteoporosis**, which leads to fragility fractures.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman had a mastectomy with level III axillary clearance a year ago. Her ipsilateral arm has become progressively swollen and heavy.
items.explanation: The more axillary surgery, the higher the risk of **lymphoedema**. That is why sentinel node biopsy is used to avoid unnecessary clearance.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman had chest wall and supraclavicular radiotherapy 2 years ago. She now has slowly progressive numbness and weakness in the hand on the treated side. MRI shows no tumour recurrence.
items.explanation: A **late radiotherapy effect** (6 weeks or more after treatment, in 5–10%) of breast/chest wall treatment is **brachial plexus damage**. The timing and absent recurrence point to radiation, not tumour.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 2.2 cm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry: ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 1+ (negative). The axilla is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which systemic treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: This is **triple-negative** (basal-like) cancer. It has no endocrine or HER2 target, so **chemotherapy** is the systemic option (platinum drugs also have a role). Triple-negative disease is also an indication for **germline BRCA testing**.
whyNot: There is no oestrogen receptor for tamoxifen to act on.
HER2 1+ is negative, so trastuzumab will not help.
Endocrine therapy needs ER/PR positivity.
A 2.2 cm triple-negative tumour carries a high risk, and adjuvant therapy improves survival.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has a 3.5 cm breast cancer with mobile ipsilateral axillary nodes. The tumour is not fixed to skin or chest wall, and staging scans show no distant spread.
questions.leadIn: Using Davidson's stage-based figures, what is her approximate 5-year survival?
questions.explanation: A 2–5 cm tumour with **mobile** axillary nodes is **stage II**, with about **81%** 5-year survival in Davidson. Fixed nodes or skin/chest wall fixation would make it stage III (52%).
whyNot: 96% is stage I (under 2 cm, node-negative).
52% is stage III (fixed nodes or chest wall/skin fixation).
18% is stage IV (distant metastases).
99% is a disease-specific figure for stage I in another source, not Davidson's stage II.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman has a 1.8 cm grade 2, ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer, fully excised with radiotherapy. Her Oncotype DX recurrence score is 9.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate adjuvant systemic therapy?
questions.explanation: ER+/HER2−, node-negative disease with a **low recurrence score** gains nothing significant from chemotherapy. The standard adjuvant drug **after the menopause** is an **aromatase inhibitor**, for 5–10 years.
whyNot: A low Oncotype score shows no significant chemotherapy benefit.
She is HER2-negative.
ER-positive disease benefits from adjuvant endocrine therapy.
Chemotherapy is not indicated, and an AI is preferred after the menopause.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a mastectomy for extensive "pure" DCIS seen on screening. Thorough examination of the breast specimen shows no invasion, but one sentinel lymph node contains carcinoma.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
options: DCIS metastasises through lymphatics in about one-fifth of cases
An undetected focus of invasive carcinoma was present
The node contains a second primary lymphoma
LCIS in the specimen has spread to the node
questions.explanation: DCIS has not breached the basement membrane, so **pure DCIS cannot reach the lymphatics**. Nodes are positive in about 2% of DCIS cases, and that is explained by an **undetected invasive cancer**.
whyNot: DCIS does not metastasise; 20% is its share of screen-detected cancers.
Carcinoma, not lymphoma, was found in the node.
LCIS is a non-invasive risk marker and does not metastasise.
Specimen error is not the expected explanation; occult invasion is.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has a hard 2 cm lump in her left axilla. Core biopsy shows ER-positive adenocarcinoma consistent with a breast primary. Clinical breast examination, mammography and breast ultrasound are all normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the best next investigation?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** Axillary nodal adenocarcinoma in a woman is breast cancer until proven otherwise. **Step 2:** Routine imaging found no primary, but a small primary can hide in breast tissue. **Step 3:** **MRI** is more sensitive in this situation and is the recommended test to find an **occult breast primary**. Finding it allows proper local treatment.
whyNot: Waiting 6 months delays treatment of known cancer.
Tumour markers do not localise a primary and are not diagnostic.
Surgery without localising the primary is not standard first practice.
A bone scan stages distant spread; it does not find the breast primary.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman had wide local excision and radiotherapy for a 2.2 cm ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer. Her recurrence score is low. She had a deep vein thrombosis 3 years ago and her bone density is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which adjuvant endocrine therapy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** ER-positive disease needs adjuvant endocrine therapy, and with a low recurrence score she does not need chemotherapy. **Step 2:** She is **postmenopausal**, so an **aromatase inhibitor** works and is standard first-line (Kumar, Pocket Medicine, Washington). **Step 3:** Her past **DVT** argues against tamoxifen, which raises VTE risk. Watch her bone density on an AI. Davidson notes adjuvant AIs were still under investigation, but current sources make them first choice after the menopause.
whyNot: Tamoxifen raises VTE risk and is generally second choice after the menopause.
Ovarian suppression is irrelevant after the menopause.
Progestogens are a later option in metastatic disease.
Fulvestrant is mainly used in metastatic disease.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and weight loss. CT shows several liver metastases, and liver biopsy shows breast adenocarcinoma, ER-negative and HER2 3+ by immunohistochemistry. Her performance status is ECOG 1.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** This is stage IV disease with a **visceral** burden (liver), so treatment aims to prolong life, and chemotherapy is used for HR-negative, high-burden disease. **Step 2:** HER2 3+ is **HER2-positive**, so anti-HER2 antibodies are added. **Step 3:** **Chemotherapy plus trastuzumab ± pertuzumab** is first-line. Monitor her cardiac function.
whyNot: Endocrine-based therapy needs ER positivity.
She is fit (ECOG 1), and effective treatment can give long survival with good quality.
PARP inhibitors are for BRCA-mutant cancers.
Bevacizumab's breast licence was revoked.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.
options: CT chest/abdomen and isotope bone scan

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman's screening mammogram shows a new cluster of fine microcalcifications. Nothing is palpable and ultrasound shows no mass.
items.explanation: An **impalpable mammographic abnormality** with a normal examination needs **stereotactic (mammographically guided) biopsy**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has a swollen, red breast with peau d'orange that has not settled with antibiotics. Ultrasound shows diffuse skin thickening without a discrete mass.
items.explanation: Suspected **inflammatory carcinoma** is confirmed with a **full-thickness skin biopsy**, which shows tumour in the dermal lymphatics.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a newly confirmed 6 cm cancer with fixed axillary nodes. Before treatment is planned, the team wants to know whether there is distant disease.
items.explanation: At **stage III or higher**, routine distant staging uses **CT of thorax/abdomen and an isotope bone scan**.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with a triple-negative breast cancer. Her daughters ask whether they are at risk.
items.explanation: Two steps: diagnosis at **45 or younger** and **triple-negative** disease are both indications for **germline genetic testing**. The result guides treatment (PARP inhibitors) and cascade testing in relatives.

questions.theme: Endocrine and targeted drugs in breast cancer
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.

items.stem: A drug for metastatic ER-positive disease in postmenopausal women blocks the oestrogen receptor and also causes the receptor to be **degraded**.
items.explanation: **Fulvestrant** is an ER antagonist that also degrades the receptor (a selective ER degrader). Tamoxifen only blocks it competitively.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a germline BRCA1 mutation has metastatic triple-negative breast cancer that has progressed on chemotherapy. Her oncologist chooses an oral drug that exploits her tumour's defective DNA repair.
items.explanation: **Olaparib** is a PARP inhibitor. It blocks single-strand repair in a cell that already lacks BRCA-dependent double-strand repair, so the cell dies (synthetic lethality).

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with HER2-positive cancer had neoadjuvant chemotherapy with trastuzumab. Residual invasive tumour is found at surgery.
items.explanation: For **residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy**, switching to **trastuzumab emtansine** (an antibody–drug conjugate) lowers the risk of recurrence or death.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with ER-positive metastatic disease progresses on an aromatase inhibitor and palbociclib. Sequencing of a new liver biopsy shows a PIK3CA mutation.
items.explanation: A **PIK3CA** mutation (the PI3K escape pathway) is targeted with **alpelisib**, given with fulvestrant.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has increasing pain in her right thigh on walking. X-ray shows a large lytic lesion in the femoral shaft destroying more than half of the cortex.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Prophylactic surgical fixation followed by radiotherapy
Oral analgesia and review in 3 months
Switch her endocrine therapy and wait
questions.explanation: A large lytic lesion with **more than 50% cortical involvement in a weight-bearing bone** is an **impending fracture**. It needs **surgical stabilisation**, usually followed by radiotherapy for local control and pain.
whyNot: Delaying treatment risks a pathological fracture; breast cancer causes about half of all such fractures.
Systemic radionuclides help widespread bone pain but do not stabilise the bone.
Changing systemic therapy will not prevent a fracture that is about to happen.
The plain film already shows the problem, and a bone scan would delay treatment.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. Aspirated fluid is a blood-stained exudate containing adenocarcinoma cells, and examination finds a hard lump in the right breast. She has not had treatment before.
questions.leadIn: Besides aspirating the fluid, what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: When a **malignant pleural effusion is the first sign of breast cancer**, Davidson advises **aspiration plus systemic chemotherapy** to treat the disease in the pleural space. Pleurodesis is kept for recurrence.
whyNot: Pleurectomy is an option for refractory recurrent effusions, not first-line.
A shunt is for recurrent effusions that fail other measures.
An effusion means advanced disease, and local surgery does not address it.
Waiting leaves treatable disease untreated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman asks whether she should be referred to a familial cancer clinic. She has no breast symptoms.
questions.leadIn: Which family history most clearly warrants referral?
options: Mother diagnosed with breast cancer at 37
Maternal grandmother diagnosed with breast cancer at 81
Father with type 2 diabetes and colonic polyps at 70
Sister with a simple breast cyst
questions.explanation: A **mother or sister diagnosed before 40** is one of the family patterns that suggest an inherited BRCA mutation and warrant genetic counselling.
whyNot: A single late-onset case in an elderly relative is common and not high-risk on its own.
Fibroadenoma is benign and does not raise risk.
This does not fit an inherited breast cancer pattern.
Simple cysts do not raise breast cancer risk.

questions.theme: Adjuvant systemic therapy in early breast cancer
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option from the list for each case below. Any option can apply to one case, to several cases, or to none.
options: Ovarian suppression plus an aromatase inhibitor

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a 1.2 cm grade 1 ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer treated by wide local excision and radiotherapy. Her Oncotype DX score is low.
items.explanation: Postmenopausal, low-risk ER+ disease needs **endocrine therapy only**, and an **aromatase inhibitor** is standard after the menopause.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm ER-negative cancer that is HER2 3+ on immunohistochemistry, with one involved axillary node.
items.explanation: HER2-positive and node-positive: **chemotherapy with trastuzumab** clearly reduces relapse. There is no endocrine target because she is ER-negative.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 2 cm ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer.
items.explanation: Triple-negative disease over 0.5 cm needs **chemotherapy**, with no endocrine or HER2 drug to add.

items.stem: A 33-year-old premenopausal woman has a 1.5 cm ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer. Her recurrence score is low and she is not given chemotherapy.
items.explanation: In women **35 or younger** with ER+ disease, **ovarian suppression plus an AI** is the preferred adjuvant endocrine therapy. An AI alone would not work while her ovaries are active.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman has a 3 cm breast cancer with mobile axillary nodes and a hard 1.5 cm node in the ipsilateral supraclavicular fossa, confirmed as metastatic carcinoma. CT and bone scan show no other disease.
questions.leadIn: What is her stage?
questions.explanation: **Ipsilateral supraclavicular** nodal disease is **locoregional (stage IIIB/C)**, not distant metastasis. Disease confined to regional nodes is still treated with curative intent (neoadjuvant therapy, surgery, radiotherapy). Some review books wrongly list this as stage IV.
whyNot: IIA is a tumour over 2 cm or mobile nodes, with no supraclavicular disease.
IIB involves larger tumours or 2–5 cm tumours with mobile axillary nodes only.
IIIA is fixed axillary or internal mammary nodes.
Stage IV needs distant metastases; supraclavicular nodes are regional.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 5 years ago has 2 months of thoracic back pain that is worse at night and wakes her from sleep. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is the most sensitive for detecting the likely cause?
options: Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
questions.explanation: Bone is the commonest site of breast metastasis (about 70%), and the pain is typically **progressive and worst at night**. The **isotope bone scan** is the most sensitive way to detect bone metastases. Plain films are used for specific painful sites because lytic lesions can be missed on a scan.
whyNot: Plain X-rays are less sensitive, although they help at a painful site.
ALP is non-specific.
CA15-3 monitors known metastatic disease but does not localise it.
Abdominal ultrasound does not image the spine.

questions.stem: An oncology registrar reviews monoclonal antibodies used in breast cancer. One drug slowed progression of metastatic breast cancer in trials but had its breast cancer licence withdrawn because it did little for survival or quality of life.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is this?
questions.explanation: **Bevacizumab** (anti-VEGF-A) slowed progression of metastatic breast cancer, but its breast licence was **revoked** for lack of meaningful survival or quality-of-life benefit. It is still used in other cancers.
whyNot: Trastuzumab improves survival in HER2-positive disease.
Pertuzumab adds benefit to trastuzumab in HER2-positive disease.
Pembrolizumab is used with chemotherapy in triple-negative disease.
Denosumab is used to reduce skeletal events from bone metastases.

ospe.identify: Mammogram (MLO and CC views): **spiculated mass with a satellite lesion**. Ultrasound: **hypoechoic, taller-than-wide mass with posterior acoustic shadowing**. These are malignant features, so proceed to core biopsy.
**Anthracycline-induced dilated cardiomyopathy** with congestive heart failure. The risk is dose-related (cumulative doxorubicin within about 450 mg/m²) and rises with trastuzumab or radiotherapy.
